name: Folkstone
lede: Folkstone is a light brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, first recorded in 1928, its spelling a step away from the English town of Folkestone.

sections.title: A name close to, but not quite, a town's
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists Folkstone on plate 13, swatch A3, first recorded in 1928 [1]. The spelling drops the middle e of Folkestone, the Kentish port town, and the dictionary does not confirm or deny a connection [1]. Our own classification places the hue in the ISCC-NBS region called light brown, Munsell notation 8.2YR 5.2/3.4 [2].

The nearest named colors on file are [[buffy-brown]], [[mocha]], [[ormond]] and [[doe]], at 2.7, 3.5, 3.6 and 4 ΔE [2]. Folkstone sits between [[brown]] and [[tan]], warmer and more orange than a plain sepia ink-brown [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Folkstone covers at least five percent of the canvas in 3,732 of them, about 15.7 percent overall, as photographed [3]. Its rate is highest in the oldest material, 56 percent of eleventh-century works and declining steadily toward the present, before settling near 14 to 16 percent from the 1600s on [3]. It is strongest in Korean, Tibetan and Japanese paintings, and its single leading companion word is Sepia [3]. These counts read photographs of varnished and aged works, not pigments [3].

origin.named_after: undocumented; possibly echoing Folkestone, Kent, but the dictionary neither confirms nor explains it
origin.source: Maerz and Paul, A Dictionary of Color
